patient.chief_complaint: Found confused and unresponsive in nursing home, brief shaking 2 hours ago, now 'awake' but disoriented
patient.history_present_illness: A 71-year-old African American male was transferred from a skilled nursing facility to the emergency department after nursing staff found him minimally responsive in his bed during morning rounds. A nursing aide reported witnessing him shake briefly — 'his whole body was stiff and then rhythmically jerking' — for about 90 seconds approximately 2 hours before presentation. He was incontinent of urine during the episode. After the shaking stopped, he did not return to his baseline. He is a nursing home resident with moderate vascular dementia, prior stroke, and multiple medical comorbidities. At baseline per staff, he speaks in short sentences, recognizes his daughter, and follows simple commands. On arrival to the ED he is awake with eyes open but stares blankly, does not respond to his name, and produces only incomprehensible sounds. His carbamazepine was recently increased 3 weeks ago from 200 mg BID to 400 mg BID for worsening behavioral symptoms attributed to frontal lobe seizures. His daughter states his confusion seems different from his usual post-seizure state — 'He usually comes back within 20 minutes. It's been hours now.'

output.proposed: Switch carbamazepine to lacosamide; evaluate sertraline continuation
interactions: Carbamazepine is known to cause SIADH via sensitization of renal tubules to ADH; this effect is dose-related. The combination of carbamazepine with SSRIs (sertraline) may further increase SIADH risk as both agents independently promote this effect.
Sertraline (SSRI class) is independently associated with SIADH; concurrent use with carbamazepine may have additive hyponatremic potential.
Lacosamide does not carry an established SIADH risk and does not have significant pharmacokinetic interactions with sertraline.
contraindications: Carbamazepine dose escalation in the context of concurrent SIADH risk (co-administration with SSRI) should be undertaken with caution; monitor serum sodium.
warnings: Monitor serum sodium during carbamazepine therapy, particularly at higher doses and when combined with SSRIs.
If sertraline is continued, periodic sodium monitoring is warranted given additive SIADH risk.
Lacosamide dose adjustment may be required in the setting of reduced renal function; refer to prescribing information.
alternatives: Levetiracetam is an alternative antiseizure medication without known SIADH risk.
Mirtazapine is a noradrenergic antidepressant not associated with SIADH, available as an alternative to SSRIs when hyponatremia risk is a concern.

useless_tools.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Amyloid PET has no role in acute SE evaluation; dementia biomarker imaging does not change acute management.
Carotid duplex is for ischemic stroke workup; SE without focal vascular suspicion does not warrant carotid imaging.
DaTscan / dopamine transporter imaging has no role in SE; no parkinsonism question relevant to acute management.

sequence_constraints.reason: CT must precede any LP to exclude hemorrhage or mass.
Confirm sodium and AED level before switching AED regimen.

critical_actions: Correct sodium gradually (≤8 mEq/L per 24h) with 3% saline + fluid restriction; avoid overcorrection
Transition off carbamazepine to a non-SIADH AED (levetiracetam) once stable
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT correct sodium faster than 8 mEq/L per 24h — risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome
Do NOT continue carbamazepine when it is the SIADH driver
Do NOT hold apixaban without reviewing thromboembolic risk — discuss with neurology and hematology
key_reasoning_points: Carbamazepine is a classic cause of SIADH; new mild hyponatremia in a chronic CBZ user can lower seizure threshold
Chronic structural focus (post-stroke epilepsy) lowers the threshold so a modest metabolic perturbation precipitates SE
Sodium correction in SE must respect the ≤8 mEq/L per 24h limit
